title: Phrasing, attack and tonality defined
summary: They define the three things DeVore's bass player says make jazz feeling: phrasing, attack and tonality.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: What's punch? How do these guys get that punch is what I'm getting at?
it's obviously not just unaccented four-four.

No. They have to do other things on top of that. Well, the punch, of course, the rhythm section is the most basic of all as far as the front line is concerned. That's what they lean on. That's the foundation. I'm not even talking about drumming right now because that's so complex and that's what makes and breaks a band is the drumming. But let's put it this way. The classical setup of a band is three-four rhythm, actually, and three front line and sometimes four if you have two cornets, two trumpets. But for a rhythm section, to be playing four-four, is the start of it, the foundation. And then these other things that the men are doing, the trombone playing the bass pedal parts and the coronet playing the lead. Our bass player, he's a pretty sharp boy. He said that on the listening that he's done, that the three things that may, I don't care what instrument you play or what you're doing, there's three things that have to be there before I have a real jazz feeling. And that's a tack, tonality, and, let's see, what was the other one? Can you think of?
Yeah. The only thing it has to be, but it has to be varied. Yeah.

Well, anything. I mean, the way a guy goes about doing something, I mean, like, for instance, a guy lombardo man can come in and play the melody straight. You know, a guy lombardo man could come in and play the melody straight, but why wouldn't it be jazz? Because he hasn't got the attack and he hasn't got the tonality. What is tonality? And he hasn't got the phrasing. Yeah, that's the three things. Phrasing, attack, and tonality.

Well, the tonality is the tone that a man makes on his horn. It's very easy for a person that's acquainted with jazz at all to hear a straight man and a hot man play exactly the same thing. You say, well, this is jazz and the other thing is, well, it's nice, but it's not really jazz. And attack is a way you hit the first notes of your phrases. And phrasing is essentially how far off the beat you can play and still retain the melody.
